sources.headline: Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery
sources.text: Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers.The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery.On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff. A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation.The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced.The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace".It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion.The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive.The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world.Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years.It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment.

sources.headline: Pope Leo XIV after his hospital stay: "I feel closer to those who suffer illness"
sources.text:
Published on
18/10/2026 - 17:02 GMT+2
Met with warm applause from the crowd of faithful who had gathered in St Peter’s Square in the Vatican on Sunday morning, Pope Leo XIV appeared punctually at noon at the window of the Apostolic Palace to lead the Angelus prayer.
Leo XIV was discharged on Saturday from Rome’s Gemelli hospital after a five‑day stay following the removal of the lower lobe of his right lung, due to the presence of a pulmonary adenocarcinoma.
"I want to thank all those who have prayed for me in these days. I really felt your support, thank you!" the Pontiff said. "I am particularly grateful to the doctors, nurses and all the staff of the Gemelli Polyclinic," the Pope continued, before describing how he experienced his time in hospital: "It made me feel in a special way close to all those who are going through illness and a condition of infirmity."
Leo XVI then said that in "this delicate phase" he will gradually resume his activities. The Pontiff is expected to travel to Latin America in the coming weeks.
How is Pope Leo? Professor Margaritora: "An ideal patient"
Professor Stefano Margaritora, the surgeon who operated on Leo XIV’s lung on Tuesday 13 October, spoke about the upcoming apostolic journey. In an interview with Vatican media he explained that there are no clinical reasons why this trip should not take place.
According to Margaritoria, at the time he was discharged from hospital the Pope was in "satisfactory" clinical condition. "The re‑expansion of the lung after the operation is progressing according to the time frame normally expected. Overall, therefore, his condition is good," the professor added.
He also said the discovery of the malignant tumour was accidental. "As unfortunately often happens, while carrying out routine abdominal tests, this small spot was found in the chest, at the base of the lungs. This is fairly common, because when radiological examinations of the abdomen are done, since the diaphragm is a kind of parachute, the lung bases are normally visible. But certainly, if this small spot had been a little higher, it would not have been seen," Margaritoria added.
The professor said he was satisfied with the operation and recounted how, in his post‑operative recovery, the Pope put "heart and soul" into it. "His determination to recover within a very short time is extremely effective from every point of view: it has truly been exemplary," he added.
"Pope Leo was an ideal patient. I don’t say that to flatter him, but he really was a patient who did not cause the slightest problem for the team looking after him," he also said.
Margaritoria then said that convalescence will take a couple of weeks and, for this reason, he believes the Pope’s trip to Latin America, scheduled to start on 6 November, can go ahead. "I would say there are no clinical reasons why this journey should not take place," the professor said.

sources.headline: Pope Leo says he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery
sources.text:
Pope Leo XIV appears at the window of his study in the Apostolic Palace overlooking St. Peter's Square at the Vatican for the traditional noon blessing after praying the Angelus, Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, a day after he returned from the hospital, where he had lung cancer removed on Tuesday.
Alessandra Tarantino/AP
hide caption
Alessandra Tarantino/AP
VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter's Square on Sunday for their prayers while he was hospitalized for an operation to remove a malignant tumor, and said he plans to gradually return to his usual duties. The crowd erupted in cheers when the pontiff showed himself in the window overlooking the square, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing he revealed that a nodule had been located on his lung, and that it would be surgically removed. ''Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers," Leo said, his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed.
The pontiff said the experience of the last week "has made me feel especially close to those facing illness and infirmity." He told the faithful that he had ''truly felt your support,'' and expressed ''particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli hospital'' where he was treated. The pope paused for a moment and waved to the crowd before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace. A delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the pope's blessing. ''He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ said Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of Congo. ″This is an expression of our joy.″ The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. He told a reporter in English that he was doing ''much better'' as he drove away from Rome's Gemelli hospital to return to the Vatican, after a shorter hospital stay than had initially been anticipated. "I don't believe it, because he was just operated on the other day," Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia, said. "It is a miracle that he recovered already."
American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization. ''I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before,'' Marsala said. "It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing.'' Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt "very blessed" to be present for the pope's return to his flock. "I'm so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong, determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this," Holland said. Leo's next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that "there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place." "The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so." Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor's genetic characteristics.

Reuters
Published: 8:03pm, 18 Oct 2026

Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter’s Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.

The 71-year-old pontiff had an ‌operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, fuelling speculation about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy.

Smiling from a window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear voice on Sunday, the first US pope thanked people across the world for their prayers and said he would now begin to resume his normal schedule.

“Having overcome this delicate phase ... I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the ⁠help of God and your prayers,” Leo said.

The pope, who was discharged from Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Saturday, came to the window ‌in the palace unaided and held his weekly midday appointment as usual.

He also urged pilgrims waiting below under cloudy skies to set aside any selfish ambitions and serve God “without compromise”.

Nuns cry as Leo appears

Leo ‌has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis was alarming for the youngest ⁠pope in decades, who was ⁠elected only in May last year.

Nuns gather in St. Peter’s Square before Pope Leo leads the Angelus prayer from a window of the Apostolic Palace, following his discharge from hospital after surgery for lung cancer, at the Vatican, on Sunday. Photo: Reuters

His doctors discharged him on Saturday after blood tests and chest imaging showed him well enough to return ‌home. They said he was able to perform normal daily activities independently.

Crowds in St. Peter’s Square, numbering about 15,000 according to the Vatican, shouted and clapped loudly as Leo first appeared ‌at the ‌window on Sunday. One Catholic nun knelt and cried, holding her hand over her face.

A few steps away, a group ‌of other nuns held aloft a sign reading, “Best wishes, Holy Father. We love you and we are praying for you.”

Pope's calendar in flux

Leo ⁠usually keeps a busy schedule, but the Vatican has cancelled his other public events until at least Wednesday, when he is due ⁠to hold a weekly general audience in St. Peter’s Square. The Vatican has not said whether he will hold that audience.

The pope is also planning to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of ‌the most intense trips arranged for ‌a Catholic leader in decades.

Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the pope’s lead surgeon, said on Saturday that Leo could be fully recovered in time for that trip.

However, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s secretary of state, has expressed scepticism. He told journalists on Friday the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward “according to the condition of his health”.

sources.headline: Pope Leo’s recovery from lung cancer surgery ‘progressing as planned’
sources.text: Pope Leo’s recovery from a lung cancer operation is progressing as planned, his doctors have said, as the pontiff received good wishes from around the world, including from Britain’s King Charles.Leo, who had a cancerous mass removed from his right lung late on Tuesday, began walking in his hospital room after respiratory therapy on Wednesday. He was eating normally, his doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritoria said in a statement issued by the Vatican.A blood test and chest X-ray showed “normal post-operative progress” and the results were “within the expected range for the type of procedure performed”, they said.The operation at Rome’s Gemelli hospital confirmed that Leo, 71, has the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma. The Vatican has not yet disclosed the results of further tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.The cancer diagnosis for Leo, who was elected as the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church in May 2025, has come as a shock.In a rare moment of Vatican transparency, the pope announced during his angelus prayer on Sunday that doctors had found a small nodule on his lung during a checkup and that it was “well-contained” and had been detected early.Messages have been sent from around the world. King Charles, who is also being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer, would write to Leo privately, a source told Agence France-Presse. Charles and Queen Camilla met the pope when they travelled to the Vatican in October last year.Donald Trump, the US president, said: “I want to see Pope ‌Leo get well. I just want ⁠to wish him ​well, get ​better ​fast.”Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, wished Leo a full and swift recovery in a message posted on X and said the pontiff was “a source of hope and inspiration for billions around the world”.The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said he and his wife, Jeanette, were praying for Leo. The couple met the pontiff at the Vatican in May.The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, wrote on X that Leo’s serenity and strength were an inspiration for all. “We hope for his full and speedy recovery,” she wrote.Before the operation, all of Leo’s appointments until 20 October were cancelled. He went on a papal trip to France in September and is scheduled to go to South America in November for a 12-day trip covering 10 cities.
